title: Technical Drawing
summary: Learn to read and produce technical drawings: drawing standards and sheet sizes, line types and tools, scales and dimensioning, orthographic projection, isometric and sectional drawings, and building drawings and CAD.
audience: Students, apprentices, artisans and anyone who needs to read or make plans and engineering drawings

body.p: Technical drawings are the universal language of engineering, construction and manufacturing. They describe the exact shape, size, materials and finish of objects so that someone else can make or build them without guessing. A clear drawing prevents costly mistakes on site and in the workshop.

list: Engineering drawings for machine parts and assemblies.
Architectural drawings: plans, elevations and sections of buildings.
Electrical and plumbing layouts showing services using standard symbols.
Civil drawings for roads, drainage and site layouts.

body.p: Drawings follow standards such as ISO standards and national versions, so that line types, symbols, dimensions and projections mean the same thing everywhere. A drawing sheet includes a border and a title block giving the title, drawing number, scale, units, projection symbol, date, revision and who drew and checked it.
Paper sizes follow the A series: A4 is 210 mm x 297 mm, and each larger size doubles the area, so A3 is 297 mm x 420 mm and A2 is 420 mm x 594 mm.

body.tip: Always state units on the drawing; in most of Africa, engineering drawings are dimensioned in millimetres.

list: Thick continuous lines: visible outlines and edges.
Thin continuous lines: dimension lines, projection lines and hatching.
Dashed lines: hidden edges that cannot be seen from that view.
Thin chain lines (long dash, short dash): centre lines of holes and symmetrical parts.
Thick chain lines: cutting planes for sections.

body.p: Manual drawing uses a drawing board, T-square or parallel motion, set squares (45° and 30°/60°), compasses, scale rule, sharp pencils (such as 2H for construction lines and HB for outlines) and an eraser. Today most professional drawings are made with computer-aided design (CAD), but sketching by hand remains essential for quickly communicating ideas.
Use clear, consistent upper-case or neat lower-case letters of a standard height, such as 3.5 mm for notes and 5 mm for titles. Poor lettering causes misreading of dimensions.

body.tip: Start with faint construction lines and darken the final outlines only when the drawing is correct.

body.p: Most objects are drawn to scale. A scale of 1 : 50 means the drawing is one-fiftieth of real size. A 6 m (6000 mm) wall at 1 : 50 is drawn 6000 / 50 = 120 mm long. At 1 : 100, a 3.6 m room is drawn 36 mm long. Enlargement scales such as 5 : 1 show tiny parts: a 45 mm feature drawn at 5 : 1 is 225 mm on paper.

list: Common building scales: 1 : 100 or 1 : 50 for plans, 1 : 20 or 1 : 10 for details.
Common site scales: 1 : 200 to 1 : 500.
Always write the true dimension, not the measured drawing length.
Each dimension appears once; do not repeat or over-dimension.
Place dimensions outside the view where possible, with small gaps from the object.
Dimension from a common datum edge to avoid adding up errors.
Show diameters with the symbol Ø and radii with R.
Give tolerances when parts must fit, such as 20 ± 0.1 mm.

body.tip: Check that dimensions add up: the overall length should equal the sum of the parts.

body.p: Orthographic projection shows a 3D object as a set of 2D views, usually the front view (elevation), top view (plan) and side view (end elevation), each looking straight at one face.

list: First-angle projection (common in Europe, many African countries and in ISO practice): the plan is drawn below the front view, and the view from the left is placed on the right.
Third-angle projection (common in North America): the plan is drawn above the front view, and the view from the right is placed on the right.
The projection symbol, a small truncated cone, in the title block shows which method is used. Misreading it can mean parts are made as mirror images.

body.p: Views are aligned: the plan lines up vertically with the front view, and the side view lines up horizontally. Height is shared by the front and side views, width by the front and plan, and depth by the plan and side views.

body.tip: Practise by drawing three views of simple objects, such as a matchbox or a step block, before moving to complex parts.

list: Isometric drawing: the three axes are drawn at 120° to each other, with horizontal edges at 30° to the horizontal. It gives a realistic 3D view that is easy to draw with a 30°/60° set square.
Oblique drawing: the front face is drawn true shape and depth lines go back at 45°, often at half scale.
Perspective drawing: lines meet at vanishing points, as the eye sees; used for architectural presentations.

body.p: A sectional view shows an object as if it were cut along a cutting plane, revealing internal details such as holes, walls and passages. The cut surfaces are hatched with thin lines at 45°. Building sections show foundations, floor and roof construction and heights. A full section cuts right through; a half section cuts a symmetrical object halfway; local sections show a small area.

body.tip: Do not hatch shafts, bolts, ribs or webs cut lengthways; standards leave them unhatched to keep drawings clear.

body.p: A set of building drawings includes a site plan, floor plans, elevations, sections, details and schedules (doors, windows, finishes). Standard symbols show doors (with swing arcs), windows, stairs, sanitary fittings, electrical points and plumbing.

list: Floor plans are horizontal sections, usually cut about 1 m above floor level.
Room sizes are given internally, such as 4000 x 3500 mm.
Levels show floor and ground heights relative to a datum.
Approved plans are usually needed from the local authority before building starts.

body.p: CAD software such as AutoCAD, FreeCAD, LibreCAD, SketchUp and Revit lets drawings be edited, copied and shared easily, with layers for different services. 3D modelling and Building Information Modelling (BIM) create a digital model from which plans, sections and quantities are produced automatically. Free and student versions make it possible to learn at low cost.

body.tip: Learn CAD by redrawing a simple house plan you know; the commands make sense once you have a real task.
